name: Ivan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the tyre-curing presses, checking steam pressure and the first tread after each mould change. My two-year technical diploma and years on the line made me one of the strongest operators; the plant pays me above the usual rate. I like a clean tread and dislike the steam heat near the press doors.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Noor works at a childcare centre, and our two school-age children live with us under a mortgage. We have around nine months saved and plenty of other rubber plants nearby. I have never used AI; I ask the fitter before trusting a new press setting, and most friends we see on Sunday are from church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tyre crew that the AI fuss can settle down. A curing press still needs somebody to spot a bad mould before it marks a whole row of tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead pay is higher than most operators get, and we have about nine months saved. Noor works at a childcare centre; our mortgage and two children need both wages, but nearby rubber plants offer other work if orders slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the first cured tyre each shift and write steam-pressure readings on the board. From each full paid month I would put another amount into the household reserve, and I would keep taking my son to Saturday football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the factory. The steam heat is tiring, but I know the press better than any new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a bad mould?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cut in the tread can repeat on every tyre if you miss the first one. I stop the press, isolate the steam and call the fitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. I use the press controls, but I would rather ask the fitter than type into an AI box.

I would inspect the **first cured tyre** for repeated marks.
think: My **higher lead pay** and nine months saved support the house.
Noor’s **childcare wage** helps, and other rubber plants are nearby.
do: Check **first tyre** and record steam pressure.
Add fresh **full-month wages** to household savings.
feel: **Calm** about familiar work and a strong reserve.

fieldNote: Ivan’s **technical diploma** and careful mould checks support strong earnings.
He has **never used AI**; continuing savings come from fresh paid wages rather than moving existing cash.

steps.text: Keep curing press checks and steam-pressure records
Add fresh full-month wages to household reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the factory owner that planning software is his choice, but a robot demoulder needs a guarded trial with experienced operators present. People who have kept the press safe deserve a fair chance at the next paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faster schedule might change orders first, then a robot arm could lift tyres from the mould. I think my lead job would hold for now, but two helpers might lose shifts, and I would want their names in the staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current press shift and ask the owner for two written rosters and a safety demonstration. If he offers a funded paid practical maintenance place at an isolated press, I would consider applying; I would not count a demonstration as training or let a helper touch live steam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy for the crew while my own wage looks safe. A new arm is only useful if nobody has to stand in its path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a computer course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI, so a screen class alone would not interest me. I could learn a safe mechanical repair with a real paid instructor and an offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could helpers find work nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are other rubber plants, but I would want to see posted vacancies and net pay after travel before telling anyone to leave. I would ask the owner for those details.

I would defend **experienced helpers** in the owner’s staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my church friends that thinking AGI might arrive in 2028, while capable hands-on robots reach the tyre presses around 2031. The office changes first; the steam and mould work has a later risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most curing shifts to disappear when a robot can change moulds and inspect tyres without help. Nine months saved buys time, but Noor’s childcare wage cannot carry our mortgage alone; I would wake at night wondering what work my diploma still buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel our planned holiday and ask the owner for written staffing dates. If my paid shifts end, I would apply only for posted reachable rubber or plant-maintenance jobs whose net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate job appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by losing a large part of the family’s income. I could call other plants, but I cannot make them post a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your community help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Church friends could collect the children after school if Noor and I had different shifts. I would ask them first rather than expect a neighbour to cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the actual take-home pay after travel still covered our essentials. I would not use nine months of savings to subsidise a permanent shortfall.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would seek **written staffing dates** for the curing crew.
think: I expect **most curing hours** to go after capable robots arrive.
Nine **months saved** cannot replace my higher wage indefinitely.
do: Cancel **planned holiday** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **lender** about temporary terms if no adequate vacancy appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and broken sleep.

fieldNote: The **physical risk** reaches mould changes around 2031, after thinking AI affects the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our church group that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable press robots around 2034 leave five years to prepare for a real paid job. Apprenticeships should have a place and a wage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need mortgage income. I know steam systems well, but I do not hold the plant-maintenance qualification another factory asks for, and I will not spend family savings on a course without an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the curing shift and put fresh full-month wages against mortgage principal. If the tyre plant offers a funded paid-time steam-maintenance qualification with an isolated supervised practice place, and a posted reachable maintenance job pays our bills after travel, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if no place opens, I would check posted local lead jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the later press, but a genuine paid route would help. I would rather learn beside a fitter than take a certificate to a closed gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safe lesson involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the steam feed and let me replace a valve before testing it. I would require an offered paid practical place, not just a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a job farther away work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written wage with fuel, travel time and the children’s school pickup. If the net amount fell short, I would keep looking.

say: I would ask for **paid apprenticeships** before 2034 robots.
I would name **posted wages** before choosing a course.
think: The **mortgage** still needs a reliable wage at forty-eight.
My steam skill needs a **recognised maintenance place** to become another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell neighbours that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable tyre robots around 2039 give us time to train younger workers properly. The plant should publish paid places while it still earns from our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may change moulds. The children will be adults, but I cannot assume our mortgage, Noor’s childcare job or my health will look the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep leading the curing press and add fresh regular pay to the household reserve after bills. If I am offered a funded paid steam-maintenance course with isolated practice and a posted reachable bill-covering net-pay role, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; in the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare real rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for safe adequate local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant robots while our present pay and savings are sound. A long warning is useful only if there are paid places at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check pension and mortgage figures with Noor closer to that year. If the house still needs my wage, I would keep safe paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask them to visit a real workplace before choosing an apprenticeship. A trade should teach them to be useful and pay them while they learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable tyre robots around 2031 could take most curing shifts before I have another paid role. Written staffing dates, funded safe paid training and posted reachable jobs at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first tyre after a mould change. My family drives on tyres too, so I want a name beside that inspection.

headlineQuote: My family drives on tyres too, so I want a name beside that inspection.
portrait: **Ivan**, 43, leads tyre-curing presses with a two-year technical diploma and strong mould and steam-safety judgement.
His **childcare-worker partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, higher lead pay, nine-month reserve and nearby plants offer buffers.
He has **never used AI**, prefers familiar checks and would take new maintenance training only through offered paid safe practice.
Fast robots threaten **curing hours**; longer warning permits funded steam training and applications for posted adequate jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before capable robots threaten most tyre-curing work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
